overview: Nguni is a family of related languages and a broad label for several societies, including Zulu, Xhosa, Swati and Ndebele communities. It was never one state. This record’s 1878 to 1914 outline lies in Tanzania and does not locate the southern African communities described here; it must not be read as their shared territory.

periods.title: Distinct societies under pressure
periods.summary: Zulu independence was attacked by Britain in 1879; other Nguni-speaking communities had their own political histories.

periods.title: Print and changing public life
periods.summary: An isiXhosa newspaper in 1884 connected readers with commerce, sport and political discussion.

items.text: Old Bulawayo in Zimbabwe was King Lobengula’s capital from 1870 until 1881. Archaeological research found a settlement combining rounded, thatched houses with rectangular brick-and-mortar buildings in the royal enclosure. A king’s house, storeroom and wagon shed show people adapting building forms to new needs and contacts.

Excavations at Old Bulawayo recovered glass beads and many cattle bones. The beads show participation in exchange, while the bones add material evidence for cattle’s importance. This is evidence from one Ndebele capital: related languages did not require every community to build the same town or organize its economy identically.

A nineteenth-century Zulu milk vessel from northern KwaZulu-Natal, now in the Metropolitan Museum, was hollowed from wood using a spearhead. Raised lugs provided a grip while milking. The narrow neck and swelling body turn an everyday container into carefully shaped sculpture that still had a practical job to do.

Milk vessels also traveled with people. The same museum account describes Zulu men taking these containers into new settings as mining and colonialism changed their working lives. An object connected with cattle could carry memories and identity into a workplace far from the household herd.

A late-nineteenth-century Nguni beer strainer at Saffron Walden Museum was made from grass fibre. Such an object puts plant-working skill beside woodcarving and pottery in the history of food preparation. Its job was to strain a drink: an ordinary kitchen tool deserves a place beside royal treasures.

Another museum piece is a wooden spoon with an ostrich-shaped handle, catalogued as Nguni and made before 1885. It is a small reminder that useful things could be playful too. The bird was part of the carving, not evidence that ostrich was necessarily on the menu.

The same collection preserves a beaded apron for young girls, a belt for older girls and a cotton skirt with beaded edging for young unmarried women, attributed to northern Nguni makers in the late nineteenth century. These objects show attention to age and dress without proving one fixed system for every community.

Written language sample: “Imvo Zabantsundu” was presented with the English title “Native Opinion.” It appears on the 29 December 1884 issue of John Tengo Jabavu’s newspaper, preserved here in an edited transcription. This is an isiXhosa title in Latin letters, not a phrase shared unchanged by all Nguni languages.

That issue includes a cricket report for a match played on 22 November 1884 between the Fear Not and Ethiopian clubs. Team lists and scorecards sit beside other newspaper material. Readers were interested in sport and local rivalries as well as large political events: a community’s history includes its weekends.

The newspaper also carried advertisements and reproduced English-language press reactions to its arrival. Those notices discuss its editor, readers and commercial prospects. The printed page gave African public discussion a visible forum while also doing a newspaper’s everyday work of connecting businesses with customers.

British forces invaded the Zulu kingdom in 1879 and defeated it after fierce resistance. Cetshwayo was captured and exiled; in 1882 he traveled to Britain to seek restoration, meeting Queen Victoria and Prime Minister Gladstone. His return in 1883 did not restore lasting peace. This was the history of a particular kingdom, not the end of every Nguni-speaking society.

When Britain annexed Zululand in 1887, the question of consent reached Parliament. William Redmond asked whether officials had actually established the wishes of the Zulu people. The colonial secretary defended the annexation by citing officials’ reports of support. The exchange records a disputed justification for imperial rule, not an independent poll of the population.

ending.text: There was no single Nguni state to collapse in 1914. Particular kingdoms lost sovereignty or changed under colonial pressure, while Nguni-speaking communities and their distinct languages continued. The end of this imported map interval should not be mistaken for the disappearance of its peoples.
